nature-eco-251.title: Ocean alkalinity enhancement: making seawater less acidic
nature-eco-251.text: One proposed answer to an acidifying ocean is to add the chemical opposite of acid. Ocean alkalinity enhancement is a proposed way of removing carbon dioxide from the air that adds alkaline minerals, or products made from them, to the ocean surface. Adding alkalinity buffers pH change immediately, which may help sea life where it is added. Electrochemical methods that strip carbon dioxide from seawater are a related form. Such ocean-based methods are still under study, with low technology readiness and many risks.

nature-eco-167.title: The deep carbon cycle: carbon's trip into the mantle
nature-eco-167.text: In 2011 a study of rare super-deep diamonds from Brazil showed that carbon cycling reaches all the way to Earth's lower mantle. The deep carbon cycle is the slow movement of carbon between Earth's surface and its deep interior. Carbon mainly enters the mantle in carbonate-rich sediments riding on ocean plates, which sink beneath other plates. This return matters for life. Without it, carbon would build up in the atmosphere to extremely high levels, so the deep cycle helps keep conditions fit for life.

nature-eco-200.title: Bernard Palissy and the discovery of the water cycle
nature-eco-200.text: In ancient times many people believed the land floated on water and that river water came from under the earth. By roughly 500 BCE, Greek scholars were suggesting that much river water comes from rain. The modern theory, that rainfall alone keeps rivers flowing, was first published by Bernard Palissy in 1580. It was first tested scientifically in 1674, in a study usually credited to Pierre Perrault. Even so, the idea did not become mainstream until the early nineteenth century.

nature-eco-268.title: Mud in the water: sediment as a pollutant
nature-eco-268.text: Soil eroded mainly from farmland is considered the leading global cause of diffuse water pollution, the kind that comes from many scattered sources rather than one pipe. The problem is the excess sediment it sends into waterways. Sediment is a pollutant in itself, and it also carries others, such as pesticides and heavy metals. Silt can smother fish spawning beds by filling the gaps between gravel on stream beds. Runoff from roads and urban areas adds sediment contaminated with fuel, oil and other chemicals.

nature-eco-267.title: Tillage erosion: when the plow moves the soil
nature-eco-267.text: On many hilly fields, the plow moves more soil than rain or wind does. Tillage erosion is the movement of soil down a field caused by plowing and other tillage. In many fields, especially on hilly land, it is a bigger cause of soil loss than erosion by water or wind. Its signature is the eroded hilltop. Water erosion removes soil mainly from middle and lower slopes, so worn-down hilltops point to tillage instead. The damage is costly, because degraded soil can sharply cut crop yields and cause economic losses for farms.

nature-eco-265.title: Splash, sheet, rill and gully: how rain carves soil
nature-eco-265.text: A single raindrop can throw soil particles up to 0.6 m into the air and 1.5 m sideways on level ground. That is splash erosion, the first and mildest of four main kinds of erosion caused by rain and the runoff it creates. Next comes sheet erosion, soil carried off by overland flow. Then come rills, small, short-lived channels only a few centimeters deep. Gully erosion is the most severe. It happens when runoff rushes through narrow channels after heavy rain or snowmelt, removing soil to a considerable depth.

nature-es-079.title: The Universal Soil Loss Equation: predicting erosion
nature-es-079.text: How much soil will a field lose to rain each year? The Universal Soil Loss Equation, or USLE, is the most widely used model for predicting average yearly soil loss from water erosion on a plot. It multiplies together factors for rainfall erosivity, the eroding power of rain; soil erodibility; slope length and steepness; cover and management; and support practices. Developed in the 1960s and 1970s, it is still the basis of global studies. It has blind spots. It cannot simulate gully erosion, which can make up 10–80% of total erosion on cultivated and grazed land. And all erosion models only roughly match real measured erosion rates.

nature-eco-266.title: Wind erosion: soil carried off on the air
nature-eco-266.text: Dust blown off distant land has been linked to declining coral reef health in the Caribbean and Florida. Wind erosion is the removal of soil by wind, a major force in arid and semi-arid regions. Wind works in two ways. It lifts and carries loose particles, called deflation, and it wears surfaces down with airborne particles, called abrasion. Wind erosion is a major source of degraded land, spreading desert, harmful dust and crop damage, especially where deforestation, urbanization and farming make it worse. Its dust is a major air pollutant.

nature-eco-228.title: Potential evapotranspiration: the air's thirst
nature-eco-228.text: Potential evapotranspiration is the amount of water a crop, soil or ecosystem would evaporate and transpire if enough water were available. It measures the air's demand for moisture. Actual evapotranspiration also depends on how much water the surface can supply. So the actual figure can never exceed the potential, though it can fall below it when water is short. The potential is higher in summer, on clear and windy days, and nearer the equator. It also defines a dry region: a place where yearly potential evaporation exceeds yearly precipitation.

nature-eco-229.title: How scientists estimate evapotranspiration
nature-eco-229.text: Water vapour rising from a landscape is hard to measure directly, so evapotranspiration is usually estimated indirectly. One approach is a catchment water balance. It relates the change in stored water to precipitation, evapotranspiration, streamflow and the water seeping down to refill groundwater, so evapotranspiration can be solved for. Energy balance methods, including the satellite-based SEBAL and METRIC algorithms, map it pixel by pixel. The Penman–Monteith equation, recommended by the FAO, calculates a reference value from weather data. Weighing lysimeters, tanks of soil that are weighed, measure it directly, but only over small areas.

nature-eco-227.title: How plants change the water a landscape yields
nature-eco-227.text: A dense forest may actually reduce the water that flows out of a landscape. The type and density of vegetation strongly shape evapotranspiration, and so how much water a landscape yields. Dense vegetation such as forest may raise evapotranspiration, sending more water back to the air and less downstream. Rainforests are an exception. While they stand, they raise humidity, cool the ground and slow winds, increasing stream flows and groundwater. Clearing them often turns land toward desert as soils dry out and erode. Deforestation also lowers evapotranspiration and so the moisture in the air, which can reduce rain downwind.

nature-eco-243.title: Legumes: plants that host their own fertilizer makers
nature-eco-243.text: Clover, soybean, alfalfa and peanut all carry their own fertilizer factories underground. These legumes house rhizobia bacteria in root nodules, small swellings on their roots, and the bacteria make nitrogen compounds for the plant. It is a mutualism, a partnership in which both sides gain. When a legume dies, its fixed nitrogen is released to other plants, fertilizing the soil. Many traditional farming systems put this to work by rotating fields through crops that include one mainly of clover. Farms that mix trees with crops can also use legumes to restore soil nitrogen.

nature-eco-244.title: Lightning: nitrogen fixed by a bolt from the sky
nature-eco-244.text: A lightning bolt carries enough energy to break nitrogen gas apart, something most living things cannot do. The freed nitrogen reacts with oxygen to form nitrogen oxides. These form nitrogen dioxide and then, in water, nitrous or nitric acid. In soil they yield nitrate that plants can use. Industry once copied the trick. Fixation with electric arcs, first described by Henry Cavendish in 1784, closely resembles fixation by lightning.

nature-eco-208.title: The microbial loop: bacteria recycle the sea's leftovers
nature-eco-208.text: In 1983 Farooq Azam, Tom Fenchel and others coined the term microbial loop to cover bacteria's role in cycling the ocean's carbon and nutrients. The loop is a pathway in which dissolved organic carbon in the sea is taken up by bacteria and returned to the food chain. That dissolved carbon leaks from many places: bursting bacteria, phytoplankton, sloppy feeding by zooplankton, and animal wastes.

nature-eco-263.title: Counting soil carbon for climate reporting
nature-eco-263.text: One model puts the organic carbon in the topsoil of EU farmland at 17.63 Gt. Under the UN climate convention, countries must estimate and report changes in stored carbon from land use and forestry, soil carbon included. Five pools are reported: above-ground and below-ground biomass, dead wood, litter and soil carbon. Reliable soil carbon estimates are also needed for schemes that pay to cut emissions from the clearing and degrading of forests.

nature-eco-261.title: Soil inorganic carbon: carbon stored as minerals
nature-eco-261.text: In arid and semi-arid places, most soil carbon is not in decaying plants but in carbonate minerals such as calcite and dolomite. Soil inorganic carbon is carbon held in minerals. It comes either from weathered parent rock, the rock a soil forms from, or from soil minerals reacting with carbon dioxide in the air. These carbonates can come from the bedrock, or form in the soil itself, when they are called pedogenic carbonate.

nature-eco-260.title: Soil organic carbon: the carbon in decaying life
nature-eco-260.text: Soil organic matter is about 50% carbon by dry weight. Soil organic carbon is that carbon, and in humid climates it is the dominant form of soil carbon. Its main source is dead plant material: roots, fallen leaves and crop residue. Substances that roots release, called root exudates, add more. Some of it vanishes fast. Cellulose, starches and proteins break down quickly, while lignin, humus and charcoal persist for a long time. It also boosts fertility: in sandy soils, soil organic carbon raised cation exchange capacity, a measure of fertility.

nature-eco-257.title: The permafrost carbon feedback: thaw that feeds warming
nature-eco-257.text: For every 1 °C of global warming, the permafrost in the upper 3 m of ground is expected to shrink by about 25%. As it thaws, long-stored carbon escapes as carbon dioxide and methane, adding to the warming that caused the thaw. That loop is the permafrost carbon feedback. Carbon dioxide from microbes respiring with oxygen makes up the overwhelming majority of the emissions. Methane forms in waterlogged, oxygen-free places, such as thermokarst lakes left by thawing ice-rich ground. There is a brake. Thawed ground grows more vegetation, which takes up more carbon, and this is the main counteracting feedback. The IPCC Sixth Assessment Report estimates releases of 14–175 billion tonnes per 1 °C of warming, counted in the common yardstick of {{ref:nature-eco-160}}. For comparison, human carbon dioxide emissions were about 40 billion tonnes in 2019. A 2021 assessment estimated that permafrost emissions would raise the {{ref:nature-clim-241}} by about 8.4%, though its methods were criticized. Researchers also debate where the rising emissions come from: ancient carbon, or faster breakdown of modern plant litter. Thawing permafrost is listed among the {{ref:nature-eco-607}}.

nature-eco-247.title: Tracing nutrient pollution back to its sources
nature-eco-247.text: Before a polluted river can be managed fairly, someone has to work out who put the nutrients there. Nutrient source apportionment estimates how much of the nutrient load reaching a water body comes from each sector, after treatment or natural losses. There are two approaches. Load-oriented methods work back from monitoring data collected in the stream. Source-oriented methods model emissions using export coefficients, typical losses measured in similar catchments. By identifying the sources, these models support proportional and practical management of polluted waters.

nature-eco-178.title: Ammonification: freeing nitrogen from the dead
nature-eco-178.text: When a plant or animal dies, or an animal excretes waste, its nitrogen starts out in organic forms such as amino acids and DNA. Ammonification, or mineralization, is the conversion of that nitrogen by bacteria and fungi into ammonia or ammonium. It is the last step of the nitrogen cycle that involves organic compounds. It runs faster where soils hold more organic nitrogen and more microbes, and where average yearly rainfall is higher.

nature-eco-181.title: Anammox: turning nitrogen compounds straight into gas
nature-eco-181.text: The bacteria behind anammox were identified only in 1999, to the great surprise of scientists. Anammox, short for anaerobic ammonium oxidation, is a microbial process that turns nitrite and ammonium directly into nitrogen gas and water, without oxygen. Despite its late discovery, it accounts for a major share of nitrogen conversion in the oceans.

nature-eco-182.title: The marine nitrogen cycle: feeding the ocean's plankton
nature-eco-182.text: Without new supplies, the ocean's fixed nitrogen would be used up in about 2000 years. The marine nitrogen cycle is the movement of nitrogen through the ocean. Overall it resembles the cycle on land, but with different organisms and pathways. Nitrogen enters seawater through rain, runoff or as gas from the air. It must be fixed, mostly by cyanobacteria, before phytoplankton can use it. Nitrogen reaching the sunlit layer from fixation, or from deep water welling up, is called new nitrogen. Nitrogen recycled there from eaten or respired matter supports regenerated production. Ocean acidification may cut nitrification and denitrification, letting fixed nitrogen build up and possibly causing eutrophication.

nature-eco-174.title: Reservoirs and residence time: how long elements stay put
nature-eco-174.text: A coal deposit can hold carbon for a long time. That makes it a reservoir: a place where a chemical is held for a long time. Residence time is how long a chemical stays in one place, and it also goes by turnover time, renewal time or exit age. Places that hold a chemical only briefly, such as plants and animals, are called exchange pools. The pattern is broad. Reservoirs are generally non-living parts of the environment, while exchange pools are generally living things.

nature-eco-197.title: Where Earth's water sits, and for how long
nature-eco-197.text: Of the world's 1,386,000,000 km3 of water, about 1,338,000,000 km3, or about 97%, is in the oceans. Ice caps, glaciers and permanent snow hold only 1.7% of all water but 68.7% of all fresh water. A water reservoir's residence time is the average time a water molecule spends in it, a measure of the water's average age. Those times vary enormously. Soil moisture turns over in 1 to 2 months, and shallow groundwater stays 100 to 200 years. Deep groundwater stays about 10,000 years. At any moment, much more water sits in storage than is moving through the cycle.

nature-eco-175.title: Box models: a cycle drawn as boxes and flows
nature-eco-175.text: A box model simplifies a complex system into boxes, or storage reservoirs, for a material, linked by flows of that material. Each box is assumed to be evenly mixed. That lets simple formulas describe how the amount of a chemical changes and where it settles. In a one-box model, a source Q flows into the reservoir and a sink S flows out. When Q equals S, the reservoir is in steady state, and its contents do not change over time. Box models are widely used to model biogeochemical systems.

nature-eco-238.title: Equations for how fast water soaks in
nature-eco-238.text: Infiltration calculation methods are equations that estimate how much water soaks into soil, and how fast, as one term in a watershed's water budget. The rigorous standard is Richards' equation. It is strongly nonlinear, costly to compute and not guaranteed to converge on an answer. Other methods are simpler. The Green-Ampt method depends on soil suction head, porosity, hydraulic conductivity and time. Horton's equation is empirical: infiltration starts at an initial rate and falls exponentially to a steady rate once the soil is saturated. The Kostiakov equation lets the intake rate decline as a power function, and a modified version adds a steady intake term.

nature-eco-213.title: Anaerobic respiration: breathing without oxygen
nature-eco-213.text: In oxygen-free wetland mud, at hydrothermal vents and inside digestive tracts, some microbes respire without oxygen. Anaerobic respiration is respiration by bacteria or archaea, another group of single-celled microbes, without oxygen. Instead they pass electrons to an inorganic substance such as sulfate, nitrate or sulfur. Fermentation is different. It also works without oxygen, but it passes electrons to organic molecules, so it does not count as respiration.

nature-eco-236.title: Seasonal fish kills: when lake bottoms run out of oxygen
nature-eco-236.text: Seasonal fish kills are mass deaths of fish when the oxygen in a lake's deep water is used up, in summer or in winter. Each season sets its own trap. In summer, the lake settles into layers, and extra organic matter speeds respiration in the deep water. In winter, ice and snow cut the light for photosynthesis and block oxygen exchange with the air, while respiration carries on.

nature-eco-215.title: What dead zones cost fisheries and tourism
nature-eco-215.text: The Gulf of Mexico dead zone is reported to cost US seafood and tourism industries about $82 million a year. Dead zones harm fisheries and other sea-based businesses, to a degree that depends on how long they last and where they occur. They cut biodiversity and bottom-dwelling populations. Oddly, extra nutrients can briefly raise catches of some species, such as anchovies. Studies estimate that gains in surrounding waters do not offset the net loss of productivity in the dead zone itself. Still, scientists do not all agree on the balance. Some argue that nutrient loading has enhanced some Gulf fisheries, such as red snapper.

nature-eco-205.title: The carbonate pump: carbon sunk in seashells
nature-eco-205.text: Coccolithophores, foraminifera and molluscs build protective shells of calcium carbonate, and those shells carry carbon into the deep. This is the carbonate pump, the hard-tissue part of the biological pump. It is one of three pumps, with the solubility and biological pumps, that carry carbon dioxide from the air into the ocean interior. Ocean acidification may weaken it. Because carbonate also helps sinking organic matter sink, a weaker carbonate pump could weaken the soft-tissue pump too.
